---
title: "Exact binomial intervals"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true

---

Normal intervals for a proportion can cross the boundaries of the parameter space, especially when successes are rare. The Hillenbrand paired vowel measurements produce such a case without invented counts.

## A within-speaker binary response

For each adult woman, define a success when /I/ in *hid* lasts longer than /i/ in *heed*. The speaker, not the vowel row, is the observational unit.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-binomial-data
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pairs_long <- subset(
  vowels,
  speaker_type == "woman" & vowel %in% c("I", "i"),
  select = c(speaker_id, vowel, duration_ms)
)
pairs <- reshape(pairs_long, idvar = "speaker_id", timevar = "vowel", direction = "wide")
names(pairs)[names(pairs) == "duration_ms.I"] <- "hid_ms"
names(pairs)[names(pairs) == "duration_ms.i"] <- "heed_ms"
pairs$hid_longer <- pairs$hid_ms > pairs$heed_ms

x <- sum(pairs$hid_longer)
n <- nrow(pairs)
p_hat <- x / n

stopifnot(n == 48L, x == 3L, !anyNA(pairs$hid_longer))
data.frame(speakers = n, successes = x, sample_proportion = p_hat)
```

The ordinary Wald interval is

$$
\widehat p\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{n}}.
$$

Here its lower endpoint falls below zero, which is impossible for a probability.

## Inverting binomial tail tests

Under $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$, the Clopper--Pearson interval finds parameter values whose binomial tails are not too small. For an interior count $x$, the endpoints satisfy

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_L}(X\geq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_U}(X\leq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
$$

Equivalently, the endpoints are beta quantiles. R performs this inversion with `binom.test()`.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-binomial-intervals
exact_result <- binom.test(x, n, conf.level = 0.95)
wald_se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
wald_interval <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * wald_se
exact_interval <- unname(exact_result$conf.int)

intervals <- data.frame(
  method = c("Clopper-Pearson", "Wald"),
  estimate = p_hat,
  lower = c(exact_interval[1], wald_interval[1]),
  upper = c(exact_interval[2], wald_interval[2])
)
stopifnot(wald_interval[1] < 0)
intervals
```

The exact conditional interval is [`r sprintf("%.4f", exact_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.4f", exact_interval[2])`], while the Wald interval is [`r sprintf("%.4f", wald_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.4f", wald_interval[2])`].

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-binomial-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Intervals for the probability that /I/ lasts longer than /i/ within an adult woman."
ggplot(intervals, aes(estimate, method, xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, 1), color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.15, color = "grey35") +
  geom_point(color = "#8B1A1A", size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Speaker-level success probability", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

“Exact” means that the calculation uses the finite binomial distribution rather than a large-sample normal approximation. It does not make the common-probability assumption, speaker independence, or connection from this screened cohort to a broader population exact.

## Check your understanding

1. Why is the speaker the independent unit?
2. Which defect of the Wald interval is visible here?
3. What distribution is inverted by the Clopper--Pearson procedure?
4. Which assumptions remain even after using an exact calculation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Each success compares two vowels from the same woman, so the binary outcome belongs to the speaker rather than to either vowel row separately. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The Wald interval's lower endpoint falls below zero, outside the parameter space for a probability. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The procedure inverts finite binomial tail probabilities, equivalently using beta quantiles for its endpoints. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Even the exact Clopper--Pearson interval assumes independent speakers and a common success probability; generalization still depends on the screened cohort's recruitment. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [bootstrap page](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd) constructs an interval for a statistic without a simple standard-error formula.
